seoTitle: How to Activate Shopify Payments as a Non-US Resident
metaDescription: Learn how non-US citizens and residents can activate Shopify Payments using a virtual business bank account and the right business information.
intro: Shopify Payments' setup wizard asks for a business registered with the government of the United States before it lets you finish, which is exactly where most international sellers get stuck. This guide follows that setup flow screen by screen, shows the billing information Shopify checks against your country, and covers the virtual US business bank account route that lets non-US entrepreneurs legitimately satisfy the requirement. It ends with the details that most often cause an application to stall so you don't lose time to an avoidable rejection.

steps.heading: See where the US requirement actually shows up
steps.body: Start the Shopify Payments setup from Settings → Payments, and step 1 of 6 asks how you're running your store: as an individual, a registered business, or a non-profit. Choosing "A registered business" reveals the catch printed right on the form — the business has to be "registered with the government of the United States," with a dropdown for structures like a private single-member LLC. This is the exact wall non-US sellers hit, and seeing it spelled out here makes clear that the fix has to be a legitimate US business or banking presence, not a workaround of the form itself.

image.caption: Step 1 of the Shopify Payments setup, where choosing "A registered business" requires registration with the US government.

steps.heading: Check what your billing information needs to match
steps.body: Further into setup, Shopify's Billing information panel asks for your legal business name, country/region, street address, city, state, and ZIP code — fields your customers could see, as the form itself notes. Country/region defaults to whatever Shopify has on file, and for Shopify Payments specifically it needs to reflect a US address tied to your business, not just your personal mailing address. This is the field a virtual US business bank account and US registered agent service are designed to satisfy honestly, since they provide a real US address and banking relationship rather than a fabricated one.

image.caption: The Billing information form, requiring a legal business name and a country/region and address Shopify Payments will verify.

steps.heading: Open a virtual US business bank account
steps.body: The fastest legal route for non-US sellers is a virtual business bank account from a provider built for exactly this — international founders who need a US bank account and routing number without living there. These services typically ask for your passport, proof of address in your home country, and basic business details, then issue US banking credentials you can plug into Shopify's billing and payout setup. It's the single step that unblocks the rest of the Shopify Payments form for most international applicants.

steps.heading: Consider a multi-currency payment partner as an alternative
steps.body: If a virtual US bank account isn't the right fit, look at payment platforms built specifically for global businesses that need to receive payments in multiple currencies without a US entity. These accounts exist to keep payments simple for international sellers and the people paying them, and many integrate directly with Shopify's payment provider list rather than requiring you to force everything through Shopify Payments. They're worth comparing on fees and payout speed against the virtual-bank-account route before committing to either.

image.caption: A multi-currency business account service aimed at sellers who need to receive global payments without a US entity.

steps.heading: Add your payment method once the requirement is satisfied
steps.body: Back on the main Payments page in Settings, the Supported payment methods section has an Add payment method button once your provider — Shopify Payments through a virtual bank account, or a third-party alternative — is ready to connect. This is the same screen every store owner uses regardless of location, which is a useful reminder that once you clear the initial registration hurdle, the rest of the process runs identically to a US-based seller's.

image.caption: The Payments settings page with Add payment method, the same screen you'll use once your provider requirement is satisfied.

steps.heading: Submit accurate information the first time
steps.body: Whichever route you take, make sure the business name, address, and banking details you enter into Shopify match exactly what your bank or payment partner has on file — a mismatch between the two is the most common reason an application gets held for manual review. Keep copies of the verification documents your bank or payment partner issued, since Shopify or your provider may ask for them again if anything looks inconsistent during a later review.

faq.question: Can I use Shopify Payments if I'm not a US citizen?
faq.answer: Yes, using methods like a virtual US business bank account or a multi-currency payment partner that satisfies the US registration and banking fields in Shopify's setup form.

faq.question: Why does Shopify restrict payments by region?
faq.answer: Shopify Payments' setup form specifically asks for a business registered with the US government, which is why it's harder to activate outside the US without a US banking relationship.

faq.question: What causes Shopify Payments applications to get rejected?
faq.answer: A mismatch between the business name, address, or banking details on your Shopify billing form and what your bank or payment partner has on file is a common reason for rejection or account holds.

faq.question: Is this method legal for international sellers?
faq.answer: Yes, the approach relies on legitimate virtual banking and payment partner services rather than bypassing Shopify's registration requirement.

faq.question: Do I have to choose a registered business, or can I apply as an individual?
faq.answer: Shopify's setup form also offers "An individual" for sellers who haven't registered a legal entity, though Shopify Payments' underlying banking requirements still apply either way.
